'''John Charles Martin''' (May 7, 1951 – March 30, 2021) was an American [[billionaire]] businessman, and the former executive chairman (2016–2018) and  [[Chief executive officer|CEO]] (1996–2016) of the American [[biotechnology company]] [[Gilead Sciences]].<ref name="BHA"/><ref name="Forbes_2010">{{cite web |url= https://www.forbes.com/lists/2010/12/boss-10_John-C-Martin_A1XN.html |title=#6 John C Martin - Forbes.com|work=forbes.com|access-date=26 November 2012}}</ref> He joined Gilead Sciences in 1990 as vice president for research and development.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://investing.businessweek.com/research/stocks/people/person.asp?personId=199167&ticker=GILD |archive-url= https://archive.today/20130118174804/http://investing.businessweek.com/research/stocks/people/person.asp?personId=199167&ticker=GILD |archive-date= January 18, 2013 |title=John Martin: Executive Profile & Biography - Businessweek |work=investing.businessweek.com|access-date=26 November 2012}}</ref><ref name="Forbes_2015">{{cite web | url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/matthewherper/2015/05/06/gileads-john-c-martin-one-breakthrough-drug-after-another/ | title=Gilead's John C. Martin: One Breakthrough Drug After Another | work=Forbes | date=6 May 2015 | access-date=27 October 2015 | author=Herper, Matthew}}</ref> Gilead is known for developing drugs such as [[Atripla]] (for HIV/AIDS) and commercializing Sovaldi ([[sofosbuvir]]) for the treatment of the liver virus [[hepatitis C]]. Martin is the recipient of a number of awards, including the [[Biotechnology Heritage Award]] (2017).

==Education==
Martin earned a bachelor's degree in [[chemical engineering]] from [[Purdue University]],<ref name="BHA"/> an MBA in marketing from [[Golden Gate University]] and a PhD in organic chemistry from the [[University of Chicago]] under the supervision of [[Josef Fried]].<ref name="gilead_bio_2013">{{cite web | url=http://www.gilead.com/about/leadership/senior-leadership/leadership-bio1 | title=John C. Martin, PhD | work=Gilead | date=2013 | access-date=27 October 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131209052944/http://www.gilead.com/about/leadership/senior-leadership/leadership-bio1 | archive-date=9 December 2013 }}</ref> He served on the board of trustees of the latter two universities.<ref name="gilead_bio_2013" />

==Career==
===Syntex Corporation===
Martin worked at [[Syntex Corporation]] from 1978 to 1984.<ref name="Gallo"/>

===Bristol-Myers Squibb===
Martin was director of antiviral chemistry at [[Bristol-Myers Squibb]] from 1984 to 1990.<ref name="Forbes_2015" />

===Gilead Sciences Inc===
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage= | audio1 = [https://www.sciencehistory.org/distillations/podcast/interview-with-john-c-martin "Pandemic Perspectives with John C. Martin"], interview, [[Science History Institute]], May 5, 2020.}}

Martin joined the American [[biotechnology]] company [[Gilead Sciences]]  in 1990 as its vice president for research and development.<ref name="Gallo"/> He was Gilead's [[Chief executive officer|CEO]] from 1996 to 2016.<ref name="gilead_bio_2013" /><ref name="BHA"/> He became chairman in May 2008, and executive chairman in 2016.<ref name="BHA"/><ref name="Gallo"/>

At Gilead, Martin helped to develop [[Atripla]], a single pill combining Gilead's drug Truvada (a combination of tenofovir and emtricitabine) with Bristol-Myers Squibb's Sustiva (efavirenz). Truvada and Sustiva were already "the most widely prescribed antiretroviral treatment regimen in the U.S."<ref name="Kaiser"/> for the treatment of HIV and AIDS.<ref name="Alfano">{{cite news|last1=Alfano|first1=Sean|title=One-A-Day HIV Pill Approved|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/one-a-day-hiv-pill-approved/|access-date=23 March 2017|work=CBSN|date=July 12, 2006}}</ref> One of the benefits of a combined pill was that patients would be more likely to consistently comply with treatment by taking a full dose of the prescribed drugs, which in turn would lessen the chance that drug-resistant HIV strains would develop.<ref name="Kaiser">{{cite news|title=FDA Approves Gilead, Bristol-Myers Squibb Once-a-Day Combination Antiretroviral Pill|url=http://khn.org/morning-breakout/dr00038487/|access-date=23 March 2017|work=Kaiser Health News|date=June 11, 2009}}</ref> The two companies announced that they would collaborate on the drug in 2004. An initial formulation of once-a-day single-dose Atripla was approved by the [[Food and Drug Administration|FDA]] on July 12, 2006.<ref name="FDA2006">{{cite web|title=Atripla (Efavirenz/Emtricitabine/Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate) Tablets|url=http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2006/021937TOC2.cfm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150827002402/http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2006/021937TOC2.cfm|archive-date=August 27, 2015|website=U.S. Food and Drug Administration|access-date=23 March 2017}}</ref> Purchase of Atripla was included in the [[President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief]] (PEPFAR) program.<ref name="Timeline">{{cite web|title=HIV/AIDS Historical Time Line 2000 - 2010|url=https://www.fda.gov/ForPatients/Illness/HIVAIDS/History/ucm151081.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150226004520/http://www.fda.gov/forpatients/illness/hivaids/history/ucm151081.htm|archive-date=February 26, 2015|website=U.S. Food and Drug Administration|access-date=23 March 2017}}</ref> According to ''The New York Times'', Gilead had about half of the US market for HIV medication manufacture by 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lee |first=Lloyd |title=John C. Martin, pioneer of single-pill HIV treatment, dies unexpectedly |url=https://www.paloaltoonline.com/news/2021/04/05/john-c-martin-pioneer-of-single-pill-hiv-treatment-dies-unexpectedly |access-date=2024-01-06 |website=www.paloaltoonline.com |date=5 April 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

In 2014, Martin led the commercialization of Sovaldi ([[sofosbuvir]]) —
"a treatment for the liver virus hepatitis C that can cure 90% of patients and generated $12 billion in revenue in its first year on the market."<ref name="Forbes_2015" />
Martin is credited with taking Sovaldi from "zero-to-blockbuster in a couple of months" with profits topping $10 billion for 2014.<ref name="fiercepharma_2015_Jan" /> 
However, in April 2014, U.S. House Democrats  [[Henry Waxman]], [[Frank Pallone|Frank Pallone Jr.]], and [[Diana DeGette]] wrote Martin questioning the $84,000 price for Sovaldi. They specifically asked Martin to "explain how the drug was priced, what discounts are being made available to low-income patients and government health programs, and the potential impact to public health by insurers blocking or delaying access to the medicine because of its cost."<ref name="bloomberg_2014">{{cite web | url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2014-03-21/gilead-s-84-000-treatment-questioned-by-congress | title=Gilead's $84,000 Treatment Questioned by U.S. Lawmakers | publisher=Bloomberg | date=21 March 2014 | access-date=27 October 2015 | author=Armstrong, Drew}}</ref>

[[Sofosbuvir]] is cited as an example of how [[specialty drugs]] present both benefits and challenges.<ref name="pppmag_2015">{{cite web | url=http://www.pppmag.com/article_print.php?articleid=1637 | title=The Increasing Impact of High-Cost Specialty Therapies | volume=12 | number=2 | date=February 2015 | publisher=Pharmacy Purchasing & Products Magazine | access-date=4 December 2015 | author=Lucio, Steven | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208051829/http://www.pppmag.com/article_print.php?articleid=1637 | archive-date=8 December 2015 }}</ref><ref name="bloomberg_2014" /><ref name="Brennan">{{cite journal |last1=Brennan |first1=Troyen |last2=Shrank |first2=William |title=New Expensive Treatments for Hepatitis C Infection |journal=JAMA |date=13 August 2014 |volume=312 |issue=6 |pages=593–594 |doi=10.1001/jama.2014.8897 |pmid=25038617 |url=https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/article-abstract/1890401 |access-date=11 May 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

{{blockquote|Sofosbuvir also is an excellent example of both the benefit and the challenge of specialty medications. On one hand, this agent offers up to a 95% response rate as part of an interferon-free treatment regimen for hepatitis C.<sup>6</sup> Generally speaking, it is more effective and better tolerated than alternative treatments.<sup>6</sup> Unfortunately, the current per pill cost—$1,000—results in an $84,000 treatment course, creating barriers to therapy for many.<sup>6</sup> Patients, providers, and payors alike have expressed outrage, and the debate has even drawn the attention of the US Congress.<sup>7</sup> Despite these concerns, sofosbuvir rapidly has become a top seller in the United States. ...<ref name="pppmag_2015" />}}

== Global Health Contributions ==
John Martin contributed to expanding global access to [[HIV]] and [[hepatitis]] treatments by overseeing the development of voluntary licensing agreements that allowed for lower-cost generic production.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alton |first1=Gregg |last2=Samuel |first2=Clifford |last3=Reddi |first3=Anand |date=2022-04-01 |title=Providing access to high-quality, low-cost medicines across low and middle-income countries (LMICs), working with governments and generic manufacturers around the globe - A business case |journal=Antiviral Therapy |language=en |volume=27 |issue=2 |article-number=13596535211068617 |doi=10.1177/13596535211068617 |pmid=35491613 |issn=1359-6535|doi-access=free }}</ref> Under his leadership, Gilead's medications were incorporated into major global health programs like [[President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief|PEPFAR]] and the [[The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria|Global Fund]], increasing availability in low-income countries.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://nap.nationalacademies.org/read/26799/chapter/50 |title=Read "Memorial Tributes: Volume 25" at NAP.edu |date=2023 |doi=10.17226/26799 |isbn=978-0-309-69653-1 |language=en}}</ref> He also worked to expand access to hepatitis C treatments through licensing agreements that made them more affordable in developing regions including in highly prevalent countries like [[Egypt]] and [[Georgia (country)|Republic of Georgia]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Jr |first=Donald G. McNeil |date=2015-12-15 |title=Curing Hepatitis C, in an Experiment the Size of Egypt |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/12/16/health/hepatitis-c-treatment-egypt.html |access-date=2025-02-02 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Varadarajan |first=Tunku |date=2017-10-20 |title=The Business of Saving Lives |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-business-of-saving-lives-1508538402 |access-date=2025-02-02 |work=Wall Street Journal |language=en-US |issn=0099-9660}}</ref>

== Appointments ==
Martin was president of the [[International Society for Antiviral Research]] (1998–2000); chairman  of the [[California Healthcare Institute]] (2005–2006, 2009); and chairman  of BayBio (1999–2001).<ref name="Gallo"/>

Martin has worked with the [[Federal government of the United States]] in a number of capacities. Martin served on the council of the [[National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases]]  (2000–2003).  He was part of the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]]/Health Resources and Services Administration's Advisory Committee on HIV and STD Prevention and Treatment (2004–2007). He was on the [[Presidential Advisory Council on HIV/AIDS]] (2006–2009).<ref name="Gallo"/>

In May 2018, Martin joined the board of directors at [[The Scripps Research Institute]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.scripps.edu/news-and-events/press-room/2018/20180515-martin-board.html|title=John C. Martin, Gilead Chairman, joins the Board of Directors at The Scripps Research Institute - Scripps Research|author=|date=|website=www.scripps.edu|access-date=31 August 2018}}</ref>

==Awards==
In 1990,<ref name="Chronicle">{{cite journal|title=Prominent group of new University trustees includes Kilts, Lansing|journal=The University of Chicago Chronicle|date=July 15, 2004|volume=23|issue=19|url=http://chronicle.uchicago.edu/040715/trustees.shtml|access-date=23 March 2017}}</ref> Martin received the [[American Chemical Society]]'s Isbell Award, "for his applications of carbohydrate chemistry to the design of medicinally active nucleosides and nucleotides."<ref name="Gallo"/>

In 2003, Martin received the [[International Society for Antiviral Research]]'s  Gertrude B. Elion Award for Scientific Excellence in 2003.<ref name="ISAR">{{cite web|title=ISAR Awards|url=http://www.isar-icar.com/?page=awards|website=International Society for Antiviral Research|access-date=23 March 2017}}</ref>  He was also an Award Winner and National Finalist for the EY Entrepreneur of the Year Award.<ref>{{citation |url= http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/ernst--young-seeks-northern-california-predominant-entrepreneurs-71762937.html |title=Ernst & Young Seeks Northern California Predominant Entrepreneurs |date=23 February 2004 | access-date=27 October 2015 |work=PRNewswire |location=San Francisco}}</ref>

In 2008 Martin became a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]], "for the invention, development, and commercialization of anti-viral medicines, especially treatments for HIV/AIDS."<ref name="Viterbi">{{cite web|title=Three Other Newly Elected Members of the National Academy of Engineering Are Part of the Viterbi Family|url=https://viterbi.usc.edu/news/news/2008/three-other-newly.htm|website=USC Viterbi|date=February 11, 2008}}</ref>

The 2014 Lifetime Achievement Award for Public Service was presented to John Martin by the Institute of Human Virology at the [[University of Maryland School of Medicine]], for his work on the development of anti-HIV medications and on AIDS prevention through [[Pre-exposure prophylaxis]].<ref name="Gallo">{{cite journal|last1=Gallo|first1=Robert C.|title=Welcome|journal=Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes|date=November 2014|volume=67|pages=3–12|doi=10.1097/01.qai.0000456047.55809.85|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 2015 Martin was named by investment firm Morningstar as best CEO. During his tenure as CEO since 1996, Gilead shares rose 100-fold, and the stock posted a 157% gain just from 2013 to 2015.<ref name="fiercepharma_2015_Jan">{{cite web | url=http://www.fiercepharma.com/story/gileads-john-martin-scores-best-ceo-trophy-huge-stock-gains/2015-01-22 | title=Gilead's John Martin scores 'best CEO' trophy for huge stock gains | publisher=Fierce Pharma | date=22 January 2015 | access-date=27 October 2015 | author=Staton, Tracy}}</ref>

In 2017, Martin was chosen to receive the [[Biotechnology Heritage Award]] from the [[Biotechnology Innovation Organization]] (BIO, formerly the Biotechnology Industry Organization) and the [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]].<ref name=BHA>{{cite web|title=Biotechnology Heritage Award|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/biotechnology-heritage-award|website=Science History Institute|date=31 May 2016 |access-date=22 March 2018}}</ref>

In 2019 Martin received the [[NAS Award for Chemistry in Service to Society]] for his tireless contributions to human health, including treatments for HIV/AIDS.<ref>{{Cite web |title=John C. Martin |url=https://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/2019-nas-awards/Martin.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190202075727/http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/2019-nas-awards/Martin.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 2, 2019 |access-date=2024-01-05 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Martin was divorced.<ref name=nyt20210427 /> He died on March 30, 2021, at a hospital in [[Palo Alto, California]], from head injuries sustained after a fall.<ref name=nyt20210427>{{cite web|title=John C. Martin, 69, Dies; Led Drugmaker in Breakthroughs|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/04/27/business/john-c-martin-69-dies-led-drugmaker-in-breakthroughs.html|last=Roberts|first=Sam|website=[[The New York Times]] |date=April 27, 2021|access-date=April 27, 2021}}</ref>

In April 2021 Forbes ranked Martin to be worth $1.1B.<ref>{{Cite web |title=John Martin |url=https://www.forbes.com/profile/john-martin/ |access-date=2024-01-06 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref>
